ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Jyväskylä.
2 Method 2.1 Participants Participants were recruited through university mailing lists, university web pages, notice boards at the University of Jyväskylä, and social media advertisements.
Participants were required to be right-handed native speakers of Finnish aged 18-40 years with normal hearing and normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
Participants were randomly assigned to either the offline or online group.
To match the number of EEG datasets across groups, two additional participants were therefore assigned to the online group.
All participants provided written informed consent before participation.
Participants completed approximately 11 minutes of listen-and-repeat practice in total over the three training blocks.
At the start of training, participants were told whether the tutor could see them.
Participants were instructed to pronounce the word aloud as accurately as possible, and the target was not presented auditorily.

Furthermore, participants were randomly assigned to the groups and were informed whether the tutor could see them only after the pre-test, so differing knowledge about group allocation cannot explain the baseline difference.

The final sample comprised 32 participants.

text.text: Social presence, particularly awareness of being observed by a tutor, may enhance learners' engagement and attention during foreign language practice, but its effects on learning and associated neural activity remain poorly understood.
We investigated whether learners' (n = 32) awareness of being observed by a tutor influences foreign speech learning in a short (11-min) video-mediated listen-and-repeat training for Mandarin words.
In the online group, learners knew the tutor could see them, whereas in the offline group, they knew the tutor could neither see nor hear them.
Tone production was assessed before, during, and after training, and tone identification before and after training.
Electroencephalography and autonomic activity were recorded during training.
Tone production accuracy improved from pre-to post-training in the online group only, whereas tone identification improved similarly in both groups.
Posterior alpha power increased during training in the offline group but did not change significantly in the online group.
Together, these findings suggest that awareness of being observed by a tutor may support foreign language speech production learning in video-mediated settings.
The accompanying differences in posterior alpha activity further indicate that the social context of learning is associated with differences in neural activity during practice.
Adult foreign speech learning is strongly shaped by prior language experience.

Nonnative contrasts can be particularly difficult to acquire when the acoustic dimensions that distinguish them are not used to distinguish word meaning, or are used differently, in the learner's first language (Best, 1995; Flege, 1995).
text.formatted: Nonnative contrasts can be particularly difficult to acquire when the acoustic dimensions that distinguish them are not used to distinguish word meaning, or are used differently, in the learner's first language <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Best, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Flege, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: Mandarin lexical tone provides a useful model for examining how adults learn non-native phonological contrasts (e.g., Gandour, 1983).
text.formatted: Mandarin lexical tone provides a useful model for examining how adults learn non-native phonological contrasts (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Gandour, 1983)</ref>.

text.text: In Mandarin, lexical identity depends on pitch height and dynamic fundamental-frequency (F0) contours, dimensions that do not distinguish word meaning in many non-tonal languages (Wang et al., 1999; Antoniou & Chin, 2018).
text.formatted: In Mandarin, lexical identity depends on pitch height and dynamic fundamental-frequency (F0) contours, dimensions that do not distinguish word meaning in many non-tonal languages <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Wang et al., 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Antoniou & Chin, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Experimental studies have shown that training can improve non-native tone perception in a short time (for Mandarin tone, e.g., Jiang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Wang et al., 1999) and learners' ability to use pitch patterns for lexical identification (Wong & Perrachione, 2007; Chandrasekaran et al., 2010), although outcomes vary substantially across training paradigms and learning contexts (for a review, see Antoniou & Chin, 2018).
text.formatted: Experimental studies have shown that training can improve non-native tone perception in a short time (for Mandarin tone, e.g., <ref type="bibr">Jiang et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Li et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Wang et al., 1999)</ref> and learners' ability to use pitch patterns for lexical identification <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Wong & Perrachione, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Chandrasekaran et al., 2010)</ref>, although outcomes vary substantially across training paradigms and learning contexts (for a review, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Antoniou & Chin, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: This motivates examining whether features of the learning context influence learning outcomes.
Social context is one such feature.

Social-neurocognitive accounts propose that learning with a social partner engages attentional, motivational, and socialcognitive processes that shape how new linguistic information is encoded (Verga & Kotz, 2013 , 2017; Li & Jeong, 2020).
text.formatted: Social-neurocognitive accounts propose that learning with a social partner engages attentional, motivational, and socialcognitive processes that shape how new linguistic information is encoded <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Verga & Kotz, 2013</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Li & Jeong, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Learning foreign words through simulated social interaction also recruits brain regions associated with social cognition more strongly than learning through translation (Jeong et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Learning foreign words through simulated social interaction also recruits brain regions associated with social cognition more strongly than learning through translation <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Jeong et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: In speech sound learning, practising Mandarin tones alongside a peer even without instructed interaction boosted early learning: participants discriminated the tones better at the beginning of training than those who practised alone, although the learners practising alone caught up as training progressed (Li et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In speech sound learning, practising Mandarin tones alongside a peer even without instructed interaction boosted early learning: participants discriminated the tones better at the beginning of training than those who practised alone, although the learners practising alone caught up as training progressed <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Li et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This suggests that the mere presence of another person might initially improve learning.
Although social aspects can support language learning, it remains unclear which specific mechanisms contribute to learning.

Recent work has highlighted multimodal information, bodily engagement, and social feedback as potentially important factors, while emphasising the need for further research to disentangle their respective contributions (Zappa et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Recent work has highlighted multimodal information, bodily engagement, and social feedback as potentially important factors, while emphasising the need for further research to disentangle their respective contributions <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Zappa et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: One potentially relevant aspect is learners' awareness of being observed by another person during learning.

In social cognition studies, being the focus of another person's attention, as reflected in direct eye contact with a live person, can direct attention towards the self and elicit selfreferential processing (Conty et al., 2016; Hietanen & Hietanen, 2017).
text.formatted: In social cognition studies, being the focus of another person's attention, as reflected in direct eye contact with a live person, can direct attention towards the self and elicit selfreferential processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Conty et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Hietanen & Hietanen, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, these effects depend on the belief that one is being seen by another person.
When participants believed that another person could see them, direct gaze elicited stronger autonomic responses and higher public self-awareness than averted gaze (Myllyneva & Hietanen, 2015).
text.formatted: When participants believed that another person could see them, direct gaze elicited stronger autonomic responses and higher public self-awareness than averted gaze <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Myllyneva & Hietanen, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: These effects were not observed when participants believed that the other person could not see them (Myllyneva & Hietanen, 2015).
text.formatted: These effects were not observed when participants believed that the other person could not see them <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Myllyneva & Hietanen, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: A follow-up study showed that physiological responses to eye contact additionally required seeing the other person, whereas public self-awareness depended on the belief of being seen (Myllyneva & Hietanen, 2016).
text.formatted: A follow-up study showed that physiological responses to eye contact additionally required seeing the other person, whereas public self-awareness depended on the belief of being seen <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Myllyneva & Hietanen, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Eye contact also increases autonomic arousal in video calls, but not when viewing a pre-recorded video of the same person (Hietanen et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Eye contact also increases autonomic arousal in video calls, but not when viewing a pre-recorded video of the same person <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hietanen et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Audience effects, referring to changes in behaviour when people believe they are being observed, have been linked to reputation management (Hamilton & Lind, 2016).
text.formatted: Audience effects, referring to changes in behaviour when people believe they are being observed, have been linked to reputation management <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Hamilton & Lind, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: However, it remains unclear whether and how being observed influences learning processes, particularly in language learning contexts.
Knowing that a tutor can observe one's performance may, for example, engage self-referential processes, such as self-awareness and monitoring of one's own performance.
Online and offline learning provide a useful contrast for examining the role of awareness of being observed.
In offline learning based on recorded materials, learners can see the instructor, but the instructor cannot see them.
In synchronous online learning, the tutor and learner can typically see each other.
However, it remains unknown whether awareness of being observed by a tutor influences adult foreign-language speech learning, including both speech production and speech perception.
The present study addressed this question using video-mediated listen-and-repeat training of Mandarin tones.
The training focused on tone production, while auditory tone identification was assessed to examine whether learning transferred to perception.
In the online group, the tutor could see the learner via the video connection, whereas in the offline group, the tutor could not see the learner, as in a recorded learning situation.
The tutor could neither hear the learners nor provide feedback in either group, thereby minimising the possibility that the tutor's behaviour would be influenced by the learners' speech production.

If awareness of being observed engages self-awareness and self-monitoring, these processes may be particularly relevant during training, when learners produce speech knowing that the tutor can see them. Electroencephalography (EEG) recorded during training allows this to be examined.
text.formatted: If awareness of being observed engages self-awareness and self-monitoring, these processes may be particularly relevant during training, when learners produce speech knowing that the tutor can see them. <ref type="bibr">Electroencephalography (EEG)</ref> recorded during training allows this to be examined.

text.text: Posterior alpha oscillations index the allocation of attention between external sensory input and internal processing (Klimesch et al., 2007; Jensen & Mazaheri, 2010; Foxe & Snyder, 2011).
text.formatted: Posterior alpha oscillations index the allocation of attention between external sensory input and internal processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Klimesch et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Jensen & Mazaheri, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Foxe & Snyder, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Alpha power decreases when attention is directed to task-relevant external input and increases with the inhibition of irrelevant input and with internally directed attention (Cooper et al., 2003; Benedek et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Alpha power decreases when attention is directed to task-relevant external input and increases with the inhibition of irrelevant input and with internally directed attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Cooper et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Benedek et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Alpha-band activity has also been linked to self-referential processing (Knyazev, 2013), and it tends to increase with time on task (Boksem et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Alpha-band activity has also been linked to self-referential processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Knyazev, 2013)</ref>, and it tends to increase with time on task <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Boksem et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: The primary outcome in the present study was posterior alpha power following each spoken word produced by the learner during the listen-and-repeat task, examined across the three training blocks (three successive parts of the training, in each of which all training items were practised once).

Cardiac and electrodermal activity, which index autonomic arousal and respond to direct gaze in video calls (Task Force, 1996; Boucsein, 2012; Hietanen et al., 2020), were recorded as complementary measures.
text.formatted: Cardiac and electrodermal activity, which index autonomic arousal and respond to direct gaze in video calls <ref type="bibr">(Task Force, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Boucsein, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Hietanen et al., 2020)</ref>, were recorded as complementary measures.

text.text: Because learners repeated each word immediately after the tutor, their productions during training could be supported by short-term auditory memory and were therefore not used as measures of learning outcomes.

Instead, learning was assessed using two behavioural tests administered separately from the training: tone production based on a written word accompanied by a tone mark, without an auditory model, and auditory tone identification.

We hypothesised that, if awareness of being observed influences learners' selfawareness and monitoring of their own performance, posterior alpha power would follow different trajectories across training blocks in the two groups.

Self-referential processing has been associated with higher alpha power, but how such an effect would develop over repeated practice is unclear; this hypothesis was therefore tested as a Group × Block interaction without a directional prediction.

Because monitoring of selfproduced speech supports auditory-motor learning (Guenther, 2006), heightened selfmonitoring could also benefit tone production; we therefore expected the change in production accuracy across the four assessments to differ between the groups.
text.formatted: Because monitoring of selfproduced speech supports auditory-motor learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Guenther, 2006)</ref>, heightened selfmonitoring could also benefit tone production; we therefore expected the change in production accuracy across the four assessments to differ between the groups.

text.text: Tone identification was expected to improve because listen-and-repeat training also involves listening to the tutor's productions (Li & DeKeyser, 2017), and autonomic activity was examined to test whether being observed increased arousal.
text.formatted: Tone identification was expected to improve because listen-and-repeat training also involves listening to the tutor's productions <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Li & DeKeyser, 2017)</ref>, and autonomic activity was examined to test whether being observed increased arousal.

text.text: 2 Method 2.1 Participants Participants were recruited through university mailing lists, university web pages, notice boards at the University of Jyväskylä, and social media advertisements.
An a priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power 3.1 to estimate the sample size required to detect a Group × Session interaction in production performance.
Because the planned analysis used a mixed-effects model, the power calculation was approximated using a repeated-measures ANOVA with a within-between interaction.

Assuming a medium interaction effect size (f = 0.25), α = .05, power of .80, two groups, two measurements (pre-and post-test), a correlation of .50 between repeated measures, and a nonsphericity correction of ε = 1, the analysis indicated a required total sample of 34 participants.
The final sample comprised 32 participants.
Eligibility was assessed by self-report during participant screening.
Participants were required to be right-handed native speakers of Finnish aged 18-40 years with normal hearing and normal or corrected-to-normal vision.

Exclusion criteria were prior formal study of a tonal language, such as Mandarin Chinese or Thai; previous participation in studies involving Chinese speech perception, production, or learning; professional musicianship; any history of neurological, psychiatric, or language-related disorders; and use of medication affecting the central nervous system.
Brief exposure to tonallanguage environments during travel was permitted when it did not exceed two weeks and did not involve formal tonal-language instruction.
Participants were randomly assigned to either the offline or online group.
Valid EEG data could not be recorded for two online-group participants because of equipment problems.
To match the number of EEG datasets across groups, two additional participants were therefore assigned to the online group.

The posterior EEG alpha analysis included 30 participants (offline: 15 participants, 12 women, 3 men, Mage = 25.20 years, SD = 4.75; online: 15 participants, 13 women, 2 men, Mage = 21.20 years, SD = 1.97).
The behavioural and autonomic analyses included all 32 participants (offline: 12 women, 3 men; Mage = 25.20 years, SD = 4.75; online: 15 women, 2 men; Mage = 21.35 years, SD = 2.09).
The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Jyväskylä.
All participants provided written informed consent before participation.
The study used a between-participants design with two groups (online and offline; Section 2.3) and repeated measures within participants.

The experiment was controlled using PsychoPy (version 2022.2.4) and comprised five main phases (Figure 1): restingstate recording, tone instruction, pre-test assessments, listen-and-repeat training interleaved with two interim production tests, and post-test assessments.
text.formatted: The experiment was controlled using PsychoPy (version 2022.2.4) and comprised five main phases (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>): restingstate recording, tone instruction, pre-test assessments, listen-and-repeat training interleaved with two interim production tests, and post-test assessments.

text.text: For all participants, both the pre-and post-test phases followed the same fixed task order: attentive listening of isolated tones, identification of tones, and tone production.

The attentive-listening task was intended for event-related potential (ERP) analysis of responses to Mandarin tones; because of a technical problem in the recording (trial-totrial variability in auditory stimulus onset exceeded 80 ms), these data could not be used and are not reported further (see Supplementary Section S3 for task details).
Resting-state activity was recorded before the experimental tasks to provide baseline measures for the autonomic and EEG analyses.
The recording comprised two alternating cycles of a 1.5-min eyes-open period and a 1.5-min eyes-closed period.
During the eyes-open periods, participants fixated on a central cross and were instructed to remain still.
Only the eyes-open periods were used to derive resting-state baselines because this visual state was more comparable to the training phase.
The two eyes-open periods were processed separately and then averaged to obtain one resting-state baseline for each physiological or EEG outcome.
After the resting-state recording, participants received brief prerecorded audiovisual instruction on the four Mandarin lexical tones.
The tones were introduced using the example word /ma/ and schematic pitch contours representing the flat, rising, dipping, and falling tones.
Subsequent identification, production, and training tasks focused on the rising, dipping, and falling tones; the flat tone was not included in these tasks.
Training was divided into three blocks.
A block was one complete run through the training items: each of the 63 tone-word combinations was practised once, giving 63 trials per block.
The three blocks were separated by the two interim production tests (Figure 1).
text.formatted: The three blocks were separated by the two interim production tests (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: These combinations were formed from 21 words (seven CV [consonantvowel], seven CVV [consonant-diphthong, e.g., gao], and seven CVC [consonantvowel-consonant]; Supplementary Table S1), each combined with the three target Mandarin tones (rising, dipping, and falling).
text.formatted: These combinations were formed from 21 words (seven CV <ref type="bibr">[consonantvowel]</ref>, seven CVV [consonant-diphthong, e.g., gao], and seven CVC <ref type="bibr">[consonantvowel-consonant]</ref>; Supplementary Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>), each combined with the three target Mandarin tones (rising, dipping, and falling).

text.text: Three of the 15 production-test words (lu, mi, and mai) also occurred in the training materials, whereas none of the identificationtest words did.
Each trial had a fixed duration of 3.5 s, comprising the tutor's production followed by a response interval in which the participant repeated the word.
The next trial started automatically, independently of the participant's response.
The tutor followed synchronized on-screen prompts specifying the target item and trial timing and therefore did not rely on the participant's behaviour to advance the task.
Productions that extended beyond the end of the trial were rare (no more than five trials per participant across the whole training).
Participants completed approximately 11 minutes of listen-and-repeat practice in total over the three training blocks.
Training was conducted through a real-time audiovisual communication system.
Participants wore standardized in-ear headphones, and a brief audio check was completed before training to ensure that the tutor's speech was clearly audible for the learner.

On each trial, the tutor produced the prompted word in real time, and the participant repeated it aloud immediately afterwards, attempting to imitate both the segmental pronunciation and lexical tone as accurately as possible.
These productions were not scored; tone-production learning was assessed with the separate tests described in Section 2.5.
Participants in both groups could see and hear the tutor.

In the online group, the tutor could see but not hear the participant (as in synchronous online learning), whereas in the offline group, the tutor could neither see nor hear the participant (as with recorded materials).
At the start of training, participants were told whether the tutor could see them.
The tutor was instructed to maintain a neutral facial expression and to direct their gaze toward the camera, and did not provide corrective, evaluative, verbal, or contingent nonverbal feedback.
An experimenter monitored the tutor's behaviour throughout training to ensure adherence to the protocol.

2.4 EEG and autonomic measures during training EEG, electrodermal activity (EDA), electrocardiography (ECG), and vocal activity were recorded continuously and synchronously using a NeurOne system (Bittium Biosignals Ltd., Kuopio, Finland) at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz, with an online bandpass filter of 0.01-250 Hz.
EEG was acquired using the EGI HydroCel 128-channel layout.
Cz served as the online reference, and electrode impedances were maintained below 50 kΩ in accordance with the system specifications.

EDA was recorded from the palmar surface of the left, non-dominant hand using two disposable Ag/AgCl isotonicgel electrodes (EL507; Biopac Systems Inc.) placed over the thenar and hypothenar eminences.
The EDA recordings were subsequently used to derive mean skin conductance level (SCL) and skin conductance response (SCR) rate.
ECG was recorded using a two-electrode configuration, with one electrode placed below the collarbone and the other on the rib cage below the heart.
The ECG recordings were subsequently used to derive mean heart rate and the root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD) as an index of heart-rate variability.
Vocal activity was recorded using a neckmounted three-axis accelerometer positioned over the laryngeal area.
The accelerometer signal was used to identify vocal onset and offset and thereby define the EEG analysis windows; it was not treated as an outcome measure.
Posterior alpha power immediately after each of the learner's productions was the primary EEG measure (Section 2.6.2).
Mean heart rate, RMSSD, mean SCL, and SCR rate were computed for each training block as complementary measures of autonomic arousal and task-related effort (Task Force, 1996; Boucsein, 2012).
text.formatted: Mean heart rate, RMSSD, mean SCL, and SCR rate were computed for each training block as complementary measures of autonomic arousal and task-related effort <ref type="bibr">(Task Force, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Boucsein, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Their processing is summarised in Section 2.6.3 and reported in detail in Supplementary Section S1.
Learning outcomes were assessed with two behavioural tests administered outside the listen-and-repeat training blocks, in the same way in both groups.

The production test was administered four times: before training (pre-test), after the first and second training blocks (interim assessments 1 and 2), and after the third block as part of the post-test.
The identification test was administered before and after training.
The posttest followed the training session directly, and no delayed retention test was included.
The production-test stimulus set comprised 15 words (Supplementary Table S3), each combined with the three target tones, yielding 45 tone-word items in total.
text.formatted: The production-test stimulus set comprised 15 words (Supplementary Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">S3</ref>), each combined with the three target tones, yielding 45 tone-word items in total.

text.text: The words represented CV, CVV, and CVC structures and were selected to be readily pronounceable by native Finnish speakers.
Participants could therefore focus primarily on tone production rather than unfamiliar segmental patterns.
On each trial, a word was displayed together with a schematic tone-contour symbol indicating the target rising, dipping, or falling tone.
Participants were instructed to pronounce the word aloud as accurately as possible, and the target was not presented auditorily.
Each item was produced once, and all responses were recorded with a Zoom H2n Handy Recorder (Zoom Corporation, Tokyo, Japan).
The same 45 items were used in all four production assessments.
Productions from the four production assessments were evaluated offline by three native Mandarin speakers.
Before rating, the raters completed the identification test used in the study, and each achieved an accuracy above 95%.

Raters judged the perceived tone category of each production while focusing on lexical tone and disregarding loudness, duration, speaker identity, recording quality, and background or technical noise.
For each production, they selected one of four response categories: rising, dipping, falling, or other.
The "other" category was used when a production was not perceived as corresponding to any of the three target tones.
Raters were blind to participants' group assignment.
The final tone category was determined by majority agreement among the three raters.
Productions for which all three raters selected different categories were treated as having no majority rating.
Across the rated productions, inter-rater agreement was Fleiss' κ = .77.
Stimuli for the identification test were generated using the iFLYTEK Xunfei Peiyin online text-to-speech platform and edited in Praat.
Four synthetic Mandarin voices were used: two male voices, Tianming and Guanshan, and two female voices, Ling Xiaolan and Xiaoguo.
The same synthesis platform has been used to generate Mandarin speech stimuli in previous neurolinguistic studies (Jin et al., 2020; Lu et al., 2023).

text.text: The stimulus set comprised words with three phonological structures: CV, CVV, and CVC.

For each structure, two words were selected (Supplementary Table S2), and each word was synthesized in each of the four voices and three target tones (rising, dipping, and falling), yielding 72 stimuli in total, with 24 stimuli per tone category.

text.text: Stimulus durations were matched as closely as possible across the three tone categories to minimize the possibility that participants could rely on durational cues.
Mean stimulus durations were 365.08 ms (SD = 58.26) for the rising tone, 363.76 ms (SD = 64.08) for the dipping tone, and 359.49 ms (SD = 63.38) for the falling tone.
A one-way betweengroups ANOVA revealed no significant difference in duration across the three tone categories, F(2, 69) = 0.053, p = .948.
Each of the 72 identification stimuli was presented once per test in a fixed order.
On each trial, participants listened to a stimulus and identified the perceived tone by pressing one of three response keys (1, 2, or 3) using the index, middle, or ring finger, respectively.

The response options for the rising, dipping, and falling tones were displayed on the screen throughout the task, and the mapping between tone categories and response keys was counterbalanced across participants.
No feedback was provided.
Reaction time was measured from stimulus onset to the participant's key response.
2.6 Data processing and statistical analysis 2.6.1 General modelling procedures Statistical analyses were conducted in MATLAB (R2019a) using fitlme and fitglme.
Categorical predictors were effects coded, and fixed-effect structures were specified a priori.
Random-effects structures were compared while holding the fixed effects constant.

For each outcome, a random-intercept model was compared with a model additionally including by-participant random slopes for the repeated factor, and the random-slope model was retained when it converged and significantly improved model fit at α = .05.
Linear mixed-effects models were compared using maximum likelihood and subsequently refitted using restricted maximum likelihood for final inference.
Generalized linear mixed-effects models were estimated using maximum likelihood with the Laplace approximation.
Fixed effects were evaluated using Type III tests.
For linear mixed-effects models, denominator degrees of freedom were estimated using the Satterthwaite approximation.
Model assumptions for linear mixed-effects models were assessed by inspecting residual distributions and fitted-versus-residual plots.
Unless otherwise specified, models were fitted using all available observations after the data-processing and quality-control procedures described below; missing observations were not imputed.
When a Group × Session (behavioural outcomes) or Group × Block (training-phase outcomes) interaction was significant, it was followed up with contrasts estimated from the same model.

These contrasts tested whether the change between two assessments or blocks differed between the groups (offline change minus online change) and estimated the change within each group; the contrasts for each outcome are specified below.
The p values of these follow-up contrasts were Holm-corrected within each family of comparisons, whereas 95% confidence intervals were unadjusted.
Effect sizes are reported as estimated differences in change on the model scale (empirical-logit units for production accuracy and log10-power units for alpha power).

Approximate partial η² was additionally calculated for omnibus effects and contrasts as F × df₁/(F × df₁ + df₂), using the numerator and Satterthwaite denominator degrees of freedom; this is an approximation based on the test statistic rather than a partition of model variance.

text.text: Vocal onset and offset during training were detected from the three-axis accelerometer recorded synchronously with EEG.

Each axis was mean-centred, detrended, band-pass filtered from 70 to 400 Hz using a fourth-order bidirectional Butterworth filter, transformed into a Hilbert amplitude envelope, and smoothed using a 30-ms moving average.
Axis-specific thresholds were defined as the median envelope plus five unscaled median absolute deviations, calculated from pooled activity 0.05-0.45 s after each trial trigger.
Vocal activity was searched for from 0.50 to 3.50 s after the trigger.
Candidate bursts were required to remain above threshold for at least 60 ms and reach a peak at least five median absolute deviations above the baseline median.
The earliest valid onset across axes was selected.
Vocal offset was defined as the end of the burst preceding at least 150 ms below threshold.
Posterior alpha-power calculation For each trial, EEG from 0.3 to 2.3 s after vocal offset was extracted.

This postproduction interval captures the period immediately after learners had produced the word, when monitoring and evaluation of one's own performance, the processes assumed to be engaged by being observed, are likely to occur, and it excludes the learner's own vocalization.
The 0.3-s delay reduces contamination from speech-related muscle and movement activity, which is broadband and can persist briefly after vocal offset (Muthukumaraswamy, 2013).

Outcome construction Production accuracy was calculated separately for each participant, assessment, and tone category as the number of productions rated as that tone category, irrespective of the tone mark of the item.
This measure therefore indexes whether learners were able to produce each tone category, rather than whether each production matched its written tone mark.
Each tone was represented by 15 items at each assessment.
Productions without a majority rating contributed zero to the number of correct responses, while the denominator remained fixed at 15.
Because a tone category could also be produced for items with a different tone mark, counts exceeding 15 were capped at 15.
Thus, the number of correct responses, c, ranged from 0 to 15 for each participant × assessment × tone combination.
Accuracy was transformed using an empirical-logit transformation, log[(c + 0.5)/(n -c + 0.5)], where c was the number of correct productions and n = 15.
The 0.5 adjustment allowed the transformation to be defined for observations at the boundaries of the accuracy scale.
Identification accuracy was coded at the trial level as correct or incorrect for all 72 trials in each test.
A valid response was required before the task advanced to the next trial, so no trials were missing because of response omissions.
Reaction-time analyses included correct trials only.
Trials with reaction times below 200 ms or above 3000 ms were excluded.
Reaction times were natural-log transformed.
Within each participant and session, observations more than three unscaled median absolute deviations from the median log reaction time were removed.

Empirical-logit-transformed production accuracy was analysed using a linear mixedeffects model with Group, Session (four levels: pre-test, two interim assessments, posttest), the Group × Session interaction, and Tone as fixed effects; Tone was included as a control variable.

This study examined whether learners' awareness of being observed by a tutor influences learning outcomes and neural activity during video-mediated listen-andrepeat training of Mandarin tones.
The change in tone-production accuracy from preto post-training differed between the groups, with accuracy increasing in the online group but not in the offline group.
Tone identification improved from pre-to posttraining, but this improvement did not differ between the groups.

During training, posterior EEG alpha power showed a significant Group × Block interaction: alpha power increased from the first to the last (third) block in the offline group, whereas it did not change significantly in the online group.
Consistent with our hypothesis, the change in production accuracy differed between the groups: accuracy improved from pre-to post-test in the online group but not in the offline group.
Because the groups differed only in whether learners knew that the tutor could see them, with no feedback in either group, this difference can be attributed to learners' awareness of being observed.
Awareness of being observed may thus improve learning from a tutor's pronunciation.
This awareness could have supported production learning in two ways, neither of which was measured directly.

Learners may have monitored their own speech more closely, a process central to auditory-motor learning (Levelt, 1989; Postma, 2000; Guenther, 2006), or they may have attended more closely to the tutor's productions.
text.formatted: Learners may have monitored their own speech more closely, a process central to auditory-motor learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Levelt, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Postma, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Guenther, 2006)</ref>, or they may have attended more closely to the tutor's productions.

text.text: Either process could strengthen the link between the tutor's model and learners' own articulation, which would benefit later production without a model.
Section 4.2 considers how these possibilities relate to the alpha results.
The online group had lower raw production accuracy at the pre-test than the offline group (Figure 2A), which could, in principle, be related to different levels of anxiety.

text.text: However, the groups did not differ in anxiety measured with the Beck Anxiety Inventory (Beck et al., 1988) before the experiment (p = .717) or in self-rated test stress after training (p = .674; see Supplementary Materials).

text.text: Heart rate and skin conductance recorded during training did not differ between the groups either (all ps ≥ .066; see Supplementary Materials).

Furthermore, participants were randomly assigned to the groups and were informed whether the tutor could see them only after the pre-test, so differing knowledge about group allocation cannot explain the baseline difference.
The baseline difference therefore most plausibly reflects chance variation.

The Group × Block interaction in posterior alpha power reflected a change across training in the offline group: alpha power increased by an estimated 17% from the first to the third training block, whereas the online group showed no significant change.

Because the underlying processes were not measured directly, we consider three possible explanations, which relate to different measures: self-referential processing and attention, which are associated with posterior alpha power, and arousal, which is indexed by the autonomic measures.
First, awareness of being observed may have engaged self-referential processing.

Being the target of another person's attention directs attention to the self, and public selfawareness increases when people believe that another person can see them (Myllyneva & Hietanen, 2015 , 2016), which was the case only in the online group.
text.formatted: Being the target of another person's attention directs attention to the self, and public selfawareness increases when people believe that another person can see them <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Myllyneva & Hietanen, 2015</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2016)</ref>, which was the case only in the online group.

text.text: Because internally directed and self-referential processing is associated with increased alpha power (Cooper et al., 2003; Knyazev, 2013; Benedek et al., 2014), heightened selffocus could be expected to keep posterior alpha power relatively high in the online group from the beginning of training.

text.text: However, the present data do not provide support for this account.
The only observation in line with it is the descriptively higher alpha power in the online group in the first block (Figure 2B), and this difference was not significant.
text.formatted: The only observation in line with it is the descriptively higher alpha power in the online group in the first block (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2B</ref>), and this difference was not significant.

text.text: Moreover, the significant effect, the increase in alpha power in the offline group, does not require self-referential processing to be explained.
Second, the alpha effect may reflect attention to the tutor and the task.

Posterior alpha power tends to increase as a repetitive task continues and attention to external input declines (a time-on-task effect; Boksem et al., 2005), which offers a parsimonious explanation for the increase in the offline group.
text.formatted: Posterior alpha power tends to increase as a repetitive task continues and attention to external input declines (a time-on-task effect; <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Boksem et al., 2005)</ref>, which offers a parsimonious explanation for the increase in the offline group.

text.text: Learners who knew that the tutor could see them may have kept attending to the tutor's productions across blocks, which could have prevented such an increase.
This account is consistent with the alpha pattern, but attention was not measured independently of alpha power.
Third, being observed may have increased arousal.

The data do not support this account, because heart rate, heart-rate variability, and electrodermal activity, which index autonomic arousal, did not differ between the groups, although autonomic measures may be less sensitive than EEG to subtle changes in state.
Taken together, the alpha effect shows that the neural state of the two groups developed differently over training, but the present data do not identify its cognitive source.
Identification accuracy improved by approximately 8 percentage points from the pretest to the post-test, and this improvement did not differ between the two groups.

This improvement is consistent with evidence that production practice can transfer to tone perception (Li & DeKeyser, 2017) and with identification gains reported in previous tone-training studies (Wang et al., 1999; Sadakata & McQueen, 2014; Li et al., 2026).

text.text: Because the design included no untrained control group, repeated testing may also have contributed.

The absence of a group difference in identification suggests that awareness of being observed mainly affected learners' own production performance, which was practised during training and visible to the tutor in the online group, rather than auditory tone perception, which does not involve observable performance.

This interpretation should be made cautiously, however, because a non-significant interaction for identification does not demonstrate that the groups improved equally (Altman & Bland, 1995), and the group effects on production and identification were not compared statistically.

The online group responded more slowly overall, but this difference was already present at the pre-test and most likely reflects pre-existing group differences.
These findings bear on online language learning.

text.text: Studies of instructional videos have mainly examined whether learners benefit from seeing the instructor: instructor visibility affects perceived social presence, motivation, and affect, whereas its effects on learning outcomes are inconsistent (Kizilcec et al., 2014; Alemdag, 2022; Beege et al., 2023).

text.text: Here, we examined the reverse direction.
The present results suggest that learners' awareness of being observed, which distinguishes synchronous online learning from learning with recorded materials, may matter in its own right.
Even without verbal interaction or feedback, learning with a tutor whom learners knew could see them differed from learning in a situation corresponding to recorded materials.
The value of synchronous online instruction may therefore depend not only on the exchange of linguistic information but also on the social situation in which learners perform.
Two extensions follow from the present findings.

First, self-awareness, self-monitoring, and attention should be measured directly, for example with self-report measures of self-awareness or perceived observation and behavioural measures of attention combined with EEG, to distinguish between the possible mechanisms.

Second, larger samples, delayed retention tests, and acoustic analyses of F0 contours, including productions made during training, would characterise the time course and durability of production learning.

In conclusion, learners' awareness that the tutor could see them was associated with improved tone-production accuracy from pre-to post-training, whereas no significant improvement was observed in the offline group.
In addition, differences in posterior alpha dynamics were observed during video-mediated listen-and-repeat training of Mandarin tones.
The cognitive processes underlying these alpha differences remain to be established.
These findings suggest that being observed by a tutor may improve pronunciation learning even when no feedback is given.
